about: P2 toy corpus (written for the P2 lesson, 2026-10-08). Made-up short documents in the climate domain; not taken from the book or the repo. Labels follow guideline v1 below. Pairs not listed in qrels have grade 0.

guideline_v1.2: sufficient: the document alone answers the query
guideline_v1.1: partial: the document gives part of the answer or a necessary piece of it
guideline_v1.0: not relevant: it does not help answer the query, even if it shares words or the topic

docs.d01: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, the main cause of recent global warming.
docs.d02: What is the main cause of climate change? Students often ask this question in class.
docs.d03: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere like a blanket around the Earth.
docs.d04: Sea levels are rising because warmer ocean water expands and glaciers melt.
docs.d05: Melting ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica add water to the oceans.
docs.d06: Forests absorb carbon dioxide from the air as trees grow.
docs.d07: Solar panels and wind turbines generate electricity without burning fuel.
docs.d08: Climate change news, climate change videos, climate change quiz: subscribe now!
docs.d09: Cattle and rice paddies release methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.
docs.d10: Heat waves are becoming longer and more frequent in many regions.

queries.q5: is extreme heat becoming more common

qrels.why: names the main cause: burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide
explains the mechanism (greenhouse gases trap heat) but not what emits them
one source of a greenhouse gas: part of the cause, not the main one
repeats the question word for word but gives no answer
keyword-stuffed footer: the topic words without any content
a carbon sink, not a cause
gives the reasons: warm water expands and glaciers melt
one reason: melting ice sheets add water
solar and wind are renewable energy, although no query word appears
names the sources: cattle and rice paddies
heat waves are becoming more frequent: answers yes
about trapping heat in general, not about extreme heat events
